items.text: Greet students.
Restart the simulation.
Ask: Do you want to play a game?
There are five identical aluminium blocks at different temperatures.
Do as shown, and let students see heat flowing from a block at a higher temp. to another at a lower temp.
Ask how temp. is distributed when two blocks touch.  Hint: Average temp.

Tell students to get a block to 5°C. Give them access to try the puzzle.

script.x: The goal of this chunk is to welcome students, and engage them in an interactive puzzle to warm up their thinking.

items.text: The gun-like object is an infrared thermometer. It measures temp.
Show students that the aluminium and plastic blocks are at the same temp. using the thermometer.
Ask: If I place an ice cube on each block, on which block will the ice first melt? Take a vote (next chunk).

script.x: The goal of this entire brainstorming is to get students to "guess" why ice melts faster on aluminium than on plastic.

items.prompt: If I place an ice cube on each block, on which block will the ice first melt?

items.text: Write down the guess with the most votes on this screen.
Test: Let students place ice cubes on the blocks, and hit the fast forward button.
Ask: Why does ice melt faster on the aluminium block? Let them pick a guess (next chunk).

script.x:
The following is a "Going Beyond" discussion.

Observation: It takes seven minutes for the ice to melt on hot aluminium. In reality, it melts much faster.

If someone asks how, say that the simulation has no air in it. In reality, air speeds up the melting of ice.

items.prompt: Why does ice melt faster on the aluminium block?
options: Aluminium gives more heat to the ice cube than plastic does in the first 7 minutes.
Both blocks give away the same amount of heat in the first 7 minutes, but plastic gives it out slower than aluminium does.
Aluminium gives away a lot of heat to the ice cube.

script.x: After the poll, say that students will test which options are wrong or not wrong just like a scientist would.

items.text: Before testing, we need to learn a fact about the two blocks we saw earlier.
Let students play and drop the temps. of both aluminium and plastic by clicking on -0.5°C.
Ask them to drop aluminium's temp. from 0°C by 4°C, and plastic's temp. from 0°C by 3°C.
Tell them to write down the values of "Heat given away," and "Temp drop" for each of the blocks.

script.x:
The goal of this chunk and the next MCQ chunk is to get students to realise this:

For the two blocks we have, if aluminium's temp. drops more than plastic's temp., then aluminium gives away more heat than plastic does.

items.prompt: For the two blocks we have, if aluminium's temp. drops more than plastic's temp., then aluminium gives away more heat than plastic does.

items.text: With the fact we have, we are ready to test!
Give access and let students restart the simulation.
Tell them to measure the temps. of both the blocks, and you write the values in the table at 0:00 using ink.
Let them first place an ice cube on aluminium, and ten seconds later, another on plastic.
Tell them to measure the temps. of both the blocks at minutes 1, 2, ..., 7, and you write their observations.
It's now time to see which guesses were wrong or not wrong.

script.x:
The goal of this chunk is to get students to run an experiment and measure the temperatures of both aluminium and plastic in the first seven minutes.

The resulting observation will help students check their guesses.
